title: Autonomous Quantum Transport Measurements of 2D Semiconductors by an AI Agent
authors: Brandon Bauer, Matthew Whalen, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, John Q. Xiao, Tao E. Li, Wenjin Zhao
abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) agents are beginning to enter experimental laboratories, automating experiments and accelerating scientific discovery. Herein, we introduce an AI-driven workflow in which an AI agent performs multi-step, multi-day quantum transport measurements end-to-end. Specifically, given brief instructions, the agent starts by planning the multi-step measurements, then safely operates the cryogenic instruments, analyzes the data, and concludes with a final report. We demonstrate this AI workflow on multiple monolayer and bilayer MoS2 devices. Through autonomous measurement campaigns lasting up to six days, the agent determined the conduction-band spin-orbit coupling energy in monolayer MoS2, and mapped a layer- and valley-resolved phase diagram in bilayer MoS2. This experimental workflow is implemented through the FermiLink agent harness, which emphasizes instrumental safety and the reliability of the measurement and analysis. The framework is general and can be readily adapted to other types of experiments, representing a step toward self-driving laboratories.
summary: This paper introduces an AI-driven framework that automates the entire process of quantum transport measurements on 2D semiconductors like $	ext{MoS}_2$. By autonomously planning, executing, and analyzing multi-day experiments, the agent successfully characterized fundamental properties, such as spin-orbit coupling and layer-resolved phase diagrams, demonstrating a significant step toward self-driving laboratories.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need to automate complex, multi-step, multi-day quantum transport measurements in 2D semiconductors to accelerate scientific discovery.
main_result: The AI agent successfully performed end-to-end measurements, determining the conduction-band spin-orbit coupling energy in monolayer $	ext{MoS}_2$ and mapping the layer- and valley-resolved phase diagram in bilayer $	ext{MoS}_2$.
method: An AI-driven, hypothesis-guided workflow implemented via the FermiLink agent harness, which autonomously plans, executes, analyzes, and reports on cryogenic quantum transport measurements.
model_or_system: The experiments are conducted on two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, specifically $	ext{MoS}_2$ (monolayer and bilayer), utilizing a dual-gated Hall bar device structure encapsulated in hBN.
key_observables: Conduction-band spin–orbit coupling (SOC) energy, layer- and valley-resolved phase diagrams, quantum oscillation frequencies derived from FFT analysis, and Hall resistance ($R_{xx}, R_{xy}$).
important_parameters: Gate voltages ($V_{	ext{g}}$), magnetic fields ($B$), and carrier densities ($n$).
main_assumptions: The framework relies on the stability of the AI agent harness and requires human experts to define robust 'Agent Skills' through iterative dry runs for new device types.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the multi-step workflow, device setups, and results showing Landau fan measurements, $R_{xx}$ vs. gate voltage maps, and the final phase diagrams detailing layer and valley occupations.
paper_structure: The paper details the architecture of the AI workflow (planning $ightarrow$ measurement $ightarrow$ analysis $ightarrow$ reporting), applies this workflow to $	ext{MoS}_2$ to extract SOC energy, and then extends it to map the complex phase diagram of bilayer $	ext{MoS}_2$.
why_interesting: While the physics is condensed matter, the core contribution is the methodology—using advanced AI agents to automate complex, multi-day experimental procedures, which is a major development in experimental physics infrastructure.
